title.en: Sharing equally: groups, multiples and factors

text.en: The dairy packs 60 packets of butter into equal groups. How many different groupings are possible?

To share things equally we make groups of the same size. 60 packets can be arranged as 6 groups of 10, 10 groups of 6, 5 groups of 12, 12 groups of 5 and so on.
Each way is a multiplication fact that equals 60: 6 x 10, 5 x 12, 4 x 15, 3 x 20 and 2 x 30.
The numbers we multiply to make 60 are its factors. The results of the tables are multiples: 9, 18, 27 and 36 are multiples of 9.
Clue puzzles in the book use these ideas. Each clue about being a multiple, odd or even, or less than 50 removes some numbers from the hundred chart until one number is left. Some clues turn out not to be needed.
(additional, not in the textbook) Sharing equally is division: 60 / 6 = 10 means 60 shared into 6 equal groups gives 10 in each group. The chapter on the Coconut Farm teaches division in detail.

problem.en: Find three ways to arrange 60 packets in equal rows.

text.en: Think of numbers that multiply to 60.
So 6 rows of 10, 5 rows of 12, or 4 rows of 15.

prompt.en: How can the same 60 packets be arranged in many ways?

points.en: Equal groups come from multiplication facts.
Factors multiply to give a number.
Multiples are results of a times table.
